1268.title: Rennyo's letters
1268.hook: the later teacher who spread Shin Buddhism through simple letters to followers
1268.howItsDone: In Jodo Shinshu temples, Rennyo's letters (called Ofumi or Gobunsho, depending on the branch) are read aloud in services, and the letter on white ashes is read at funerals.

segments.voice: Evening in a farming village in Japan, long ago. The work is done, and neighbors crowd into one house. Someone unfolds a sheet of paper and reads it aloud, slowly, so the people at the back can hear. It isn't a learned treatise full of Chinese characters that only monks can follow. It's written in plain Japanese, in the simple script ordinary people could read, and it says the important thing in a few lines. When the reading ends, the room says the name together. The letter came from a teacher named Rennyo.
screen: `EVENING IN A FARMING VILLAGE.` → `A LETTER READ ALOUD.` → `PLAIN WORDS, THEN THE NAME.`

segments.voice: First, who he was. Rennyo came generations after Shinran, a descendant who became head of the Honganji, the temple that grew from Shinran's grave. Tradition remembers him as the teacher who carried Shin Buddhism out of a small circle and into villages across Japan. Second, his tool: the letter. Rennyo wrote to followers in plain Japanese, in the simple script, not the dense Chinese of scholars. Tradition says his letters were copied by hand, carried from village to village, and read aloud in gatherings. Shin Buddhists still read them in services; one branch calls them Ofumi, the letters, and another Gobunsho. Third, what the letters keep saying. Again and again they return to a short core: entrust yourself to Amida with a single heart, let go of trying to earn your way, then say the name in thanks. He didn't add new layers. He kept taking layers off. Fourth, the letter people know best, often called the letter on white ashes. It says, in effect: in the morning we may have rosy cheeks, and by evening be white ashes. Life is that short and that uncertain, so don't put off the one thing that matters. It is read aloud at Shin funerals. Rennyo's gift was not a new idea. It was plainness: the deep thing said in words a tired farmer could hear after dark, and remember the next morning.

1269.title: Chan and Pure Land together
1269.hook: in China and Vietnam many practice both: sitting and calling the name
1269.howItsDone: In some Chinese and Vietnamese monasteries and temples, practitioners combine sitting meditation with chanting Amitabha's name, sometimes holding the question 'who is reciting the Buddha's name?' while they chant.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SIXTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rennyo's letters: plain Japanese, read aloud after dark, and the letter on white ashes. Your line was simple letters.
screen: `SIMPLE LETTERS.`

segments.voice: Sit in silence, or call the name? In a monastery in China, nobody is asked to choose. In the morning the meditation hall is silent; rows of monks and laypeople sit, nobody speaking, the incense burning down. That afternoon, the same people are on their feet in another hall, walking slowly around an image of Amitabha, chanting Namo Amituofo, Amituofo, Amituofo, over and over. Nobody has switched schools at lunch. Today: Chan and Pure Land together.
screen: `MORNING: SILENT SITTING.` → `AFTERNOON: CHANTING THE NAME.` → `THE SAME PEOPLE, ONE ROOF.`

segments.voice: First, where this happens. In Japan, Zen and Pure Land grew into separate schools with separate temples. In China and Vietnam the story went differently: you can find monasteries and temples where sitting meditation and calling the name live side by side, practiced by the same people on the same day. Vietnamese Thien, from the end of the Zen weeks, is one example. Second, a verse. Tradition credits a Chinese teacher, Yongming Yanshou, with a verse on the two practices. Its image: someone who has both Chan and Pure Land is like a tiger that has grown horns, strength with more strength added. Third, a question that joins them. Some Chan teachers in China gave students who chant the name a question to hold: who is it that is reciting the Buddha's name? The chanting goes on, and underneath it the question turns back on the one chanting. A Pure Land practice becomes a Chan question, and neither is dropped. Fourth, how practitioners describe the fit. Some say sitting quiets the mind, and the name gives it somewhere to rest. Teachers don't all agree on how the two relate: some treat the name as the main practice and sitting as support, others the reverse. But on an ordinary afternoon in a temple in Hanoi or Taipei, nobody needs to settle it first.
screen: `SEPARATE IN JAPAN, ONE ROOF ELSEWHERE.` · `A TIGER THAT HAS GROWN HORNS.` · `WHO IS RECITING THE NAME?` · `SITTING QUIETS; THE NAME GIVES REST.` · then, large: `BOTH TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: For the first minute, just sit, feel the breath, and let the mind go quiet, the way it did in the Zen weeks. Then, if you'd like, say Namo Amituofo softly, once on each out-breath, or listen to the name inside if you'd rather not chant. Once, partway through, ask quietly: who is saying this? Don't answer; keep going.

1270.title: At the end of life
1270.hook: Pure Land practice at the deathbed: the name said with the dying
1270.howItsDone: In Chinese Pure Land communities, family and temple members take turns chanting Amitabha's name at the bedside of the dying; Japanese Pure Land traditions have their own deathbed rites, and in Shin Buddhism, where birth is understood as settled in life, the nembutsu is said at the end in gratitude.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chan and Pure Land together: silent sitting in the morning, the name in the afternoon, a tiger with horns. Your line was both together.

segments.voice: A hospital room, late at night. An old woman lies still, her breathing slow and shallow. Around the bed, her family and a few friends from the temple stand close, chanting softly, steadily: Amituofo, Amituofo. When one voice tires, another picks it up. She may not be able to speak anymore, or even open her eyes. But the name keeps going, just above her, like a handrail she can reach for in the dark. Today: at the end of life.
screen: `A HOSPITAL ROOM, LATE AT NIGHT.` → `FAMILY CHANTING SOFTLY.` → `THE NAME LIKE A HANDRAIL.`

segments.voice: First, the root, from a week ago: in the Contemplation Sutra, a dying man too pressed by pain to picture anything, and a good friend at his side who tells him to just say the name. Some Pure Land teachers trace deathbed practice to that friend. The point isn't only what the dying person can do. It's who is sitting with them. Second, in China. Chanting the name with and for the dying has its own name, zhunian, helping recitation. People take turns, so the name never stops, and the dying person can follow it with their mind even without the breath to say it. Third, in Japan. Tradition says the monk Genshin, in his book on birth in the Pure Land, described deathbed rites: an image of Amida set facing west, and colored threads tied from the image's hand to the hand of the dying, a thread to hold on the way. Fourth, where teachers differ. For Shinran, birth in the Pure Land is settled in this life, the moment shinjin is given. So in Shin Buddhism the last hour is not a test, and there's no need to wait anxiously for Amida to come at death. Other Pure Land communities place great weight on the deathbed and the last thought of the name. Both do the same simple thing for the person in the bed: they don't leave them alone with the dark.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who is ill, or old, or near the end, or someone who has already died; if no one comes, hold a stranger in a hospital bed tonight. Picture them resting in a soft, wide light, the way Pure Land Buddhists picture the light of Amitabha. If you say the name, say it for them quietly; if not, just keep them company in your mind. And if a loss feels too heavy to carry alone, you don't have to: in the US you can call or text 988, or reach local emergency help where you are.

1271.title: The wonderful good people
1271.hook: humble Shin followers remembered for their joyful faith, like the clog-maker Saichi
1271.howItsDone: Shin Buddhists tell and read stories of myokonin, humble followers known for joyful entrusting, and Saichi's simple nembutsu verses are read in Shin communities and beyond.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, at the end of life: voices taking turns at a bedside so the name never stops. Your line was the name at the end.
screen: `THE NAME AT THE END.`

segments.voice: Saichi made wooden clogs for a living, in a small seaside town in Japan. He sits at his bench shaping them, the kind with two wooden teeth underneath. His plane pulls long pale curls of wood off the block, and they pile up on the floor. Every so often he stops, picks up a shaving, and writes a few words on it with a brush. Then back to work. Tradition says that at the end of the day, he copied the words from the shavings into notebooks. They were poems, simple ones, and again and again they came back to the name: Namu Amida Butsu. Today's word is what Shin Buddhists call people like him: myokonin.
screen: `A CLOG-MAKER AT HIS BENCH.` → `WORDS ON WOOD SHAVINGS.` → `ENDING WITH THE NAME.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Myokonin means wonderful good people. Shin Buddhists use it for ordinary followers, farmers, shopkeepers, servants, craftsmen, remembered not for learning or rank but for the joy and simplicity of their entrusting. Stories about them were collected and passed around, the way other traditions pass around stories of saints. Second, Saichi himself, a clog-maker who never became a priest or a scholar. His verses talk to Amida the way you'd talk to someone in the next room: plain, sometimes funny, and some end in the name, as if the poem ran out of words and the nembutsu took over. Later, the writer D. T. Suzuki brought Saichi's verses to readers far beyond his town. Third, what's surprising. These aren't the verses of a man who thinks he has become good. Saichi writes bluntly about his own faults, his craving, his temper, the ordinary mess of a person, and right beside that, the joy. That's this week's pattern, lived at a workbench: Shinran's honesty about passions, the trust that is given rather than built, the name said in thanks. Fourth, why the tradition holds them up. In its telling, a myokonin shows that this path doesn't need a monastery or a library. It can happen to a man with sawdust on his sleeves. The teaching Rennyo sent out in plain letters came back, in Saichi, written on scraps of wood.

1272.title: Pure Land in the West
1272.hook: Japanese American Buddhist churches and Chinese temples far from Asia
1272.howItsDone: Japanese American Shin Buddhist temples, some called Buddhist churches, hold Sunday services with chanting of the nembutsu, Dharma school and a summer Obon festival; Chinese Pure Land temples outside Asia hold chanting services and use Amituofo as a greeting.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the myokonin, the wonderful good people of Shin Buddhism, like the clog-maker Saichi, who wrote his poems on shavings of wood. Your line was the clog-maker's joy.
screen: `THE CLOG-MAKER'S JOY.`

segments.voice: Paper lanterns are strung across a parking lot on a summer evening in California. Families in light cotton robes and sneakers move in a slow circle while a big drum keeps the time. Behind them stands a plain building with a sign that reads Buddhist Church. On Sunday morning, people will sit in pews there and chant Namu Amida Butsu. In another city, a Chinese temple wedged between a bakery and a dry cleaner has a red door, a cloud of incense, and the words Namo Amituofo by the entrance. The teaching of the land of bliss crossed an ocean in the luggage of ordinary people. Today: Pure Land in the West.
screen: `LANTERNS OVER A PARKING LOT.` → `A SIGN THAT READS BUDDHIST CHURCH.` → `PURE LAND IN THE WEST.`

segments.voice: First, the direction. The Pure Land sutras place Amitabha's land in the west. In the Smaller Sukhavati-vyuha, the Buddha tells Shariputra about a world far off to the west, called Sukhavati, where Amitabha teaches now. Tradition says people faced the setting sun to remember it. Families from Japan and China moved east across the Pacific, and the West became a new home: Hawaii, California, Canada. Second, the buildings. Japanese immigrant families, among them Shin Buddhists, built temples in their new towns, and some of those temples took the name church. They added pews, Sunday services, a Dharma school for the children, and songs in English beside the old chants. Some readers see that as giving something up. Some members describe it the other way: the shape changed so the teaching could stay. Third, what a temple did for people far from home. It was a kitchen and a meal hall. It kept the old language alive for grandparents and taught it to grandchildren. It held funerals, weddings, and the summer Obon festival, where the dead are remembered with dancing. Chinese temples did much the same, with chanting, vegetarian meals, and Amituofo said as a greeting and a thank-you. Fourth, why this teaching traveled so well. The nembutsu needs no building at all. It fits inside one breath, in a kitchen in Ohio or a hospital room in Toronto: the one thing those families could carry without a crate or a ticket.

1273.title: This world as practice
1273.hook: many teachers say the Pure Land also points to a mind made pure here
1273.howItsDone: Some Pure Land and Chan teachers in East Asia pair calling Amitabha's name with the teaching, from the Vimalakirti Sutra, that as the mind is purified the land is purified, so daily life itself becomes a place of practice.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pure Land in the West: temples with pews, lanterns over a parking lot, the name said far from Asia. Your line was far from home.
screen: `FAR FROM HOME.`

segments.voice: Shariputra had a worry, and in the Vimalakirti Sutra he keeps it to himself. If a buddha's land is pure when his mind is pure, he wonders, then why does this world look the way it does? Hills and pits, thorns and gravel, dirt and mess. The Buddha hears the thought anyway. He presses the ground with his toe, and for a moment the whole world shows itself covered in jewels. Then he says, more or less: it was always like this. You just weren't seeing it. Today: this world as practice.
screen: `SHARIPUTRA'S QUIET WORRY.` → `A TOE PRESSES THE GROUND.` → `THIS WORLD AS PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: First, the line that sets it up. Just before that scene, the Vimalakirti Sutra has the Buddha say, in effect, that a bodhisattva who wants a pure land should purify the mind, because as the mind is purified, the land is purified. Some teachers in East Asia read the Pure Land sutras with that line in their ear. The land of bliss in the west is real to them, and it also points at something closer: a mind made pure, here. Second, the toe. Shariputra wasn't wrong about the gravel. The sutra doesn't say the thorns are imaginary. It says the same ground looks different depending on who is looking. The work isn't to move somewhere cleaner. It's to see this place clearly. Third, an older echo. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, sums up the teaching in one breath: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened." Purifying the mind isn't a Pure Land invention; it sits in a verse that says nothing about a land in the west. Fourth, what this looks like on a Tuesday. A pure mind, here, isn't a spotless mind. It's a moment met without the extra layer: the grudge, the rush, the story about how this shouldn't be happening. Washing a pan without resenting it. Answering a message without the sharp edge. For these teachers, that small clean moment is a glimpse of the land itself. Tomorrow: how Pure Land teachers answer differently about where the land really is.
screen: `AS THE MIND IS PURE, THE LAND IS PURE.` · `THE SAME GROUND, SEEN CLEARLY.` · `AN OLDER ECHO: PURIFY ONE'S MIND.` · `ONE CLEAN MOMENT, HERE.` · then, large: `PURE HERE.`

segments.voice: When the next small moment comes, a sip of water, a step, a breath, do just that one thing, with nothing added: no commentary, no hurry, no complaint. Then do it again with the next one. If a grudge or a worry slips in, notice it, and let the next breath be clean.
This world as practice. The teaching that the Pure Land also points to a mind made pure right here, so ordinary ground becomes the place of practice. Today's word.
screen: `THIS WORLD AS PRACTICE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: pure here. The same ground, seen clearly. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1273 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: MANY VIEWS OF THE LAND.`

1274.title: Many views of the land
1274.hook: a real land, a state of mind, or both: Pure Land teachers answer differently
1274.howItsDone: Pure Land Buddhists hold different views of the Pure Land, as a real land in the west, as the purified mind, or as both, and they share the practice of calling Amitabha's name.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, this world as practice: the Buddha's toe on the ground, and a mind made pure right here. Your line was pure here.
screen: `PURE HERE.`

segments.voice: Here's a question you could ask at the end of a temple service, over tea and rice crackers. Is the Pure Land a real place? Ask three Pure Land teachers and you may get three answers. One says yes: a land in the west, prepared by Amitabha's vows, where those who call his name are born. One says it's the mind itself, made pure. One smiles, says both, and pours more tea. Today: many views of the land.
screen: `IS THE PURE LAND A REAL PLACE?` → `THREE TEACHERS, THREE ANSWERS.` → `MANY VIEWS OF THE LAND.`

segments.voice: First view: a real land. The Pure Land sutras describe Sukhavati in detail, its jeweled trees, its lotus ponds, its birds whose songs are the teaching, and place it far to the west. Shandao, the Chinese teacher you met earlier, is remembered for taking those descriptions seriously, as a land one is born into at the end of this life. For people who hold this view, the promise is plain and concrete: there is somewhere to go, and Amitabha is there. Second view: the mind. Some Chan teachers spoke of the Pure Land of mind only. On this reading, the land of bliss is what the mind becomes when greed and anger fall away, and the sutra's jewels are pictures of that. Yesterday's line from the Vimalakirti Sutra, as the mind is purified the land is purified, sits behind this view. Third view: both, in another key. Shinran, the founder of Jodo Shinshu, taught that when true entrusting, shinjin, is settled, birth in the Pure Land is settled too, already, in this life. The land is still Amitabha's land, and its light is already at work in an ordinary person here. Fourth, how the tradition holds the difference. These views live side by side, sometimes in the same temple, sometimes in the same person over a lifetime. Teachers argue about them, carefully. But the practice is shared: the name, said with trust. Nobody has to settle the map before saying Namu Amida Butsu.
screen: `A REAL LAND IN THE WEST.` · `THE PURE LAND OF MIND ONLY.` · `SETTLED NOW, BORN THERE.` · `THE NAME COMES BEFORE THE MAP.` · then, large: `MORE THAN ONE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands on your knees, palms up. In the right, place a real land far to the west, full of light; in the left, a mind made clear, right here. Don't choose; just hold both calmly as you breathe, and if one hand feels heavier, keep holding the other anyway.
Many views of the land. Pure Land teachers answer differently: a real land in the west, the mind made pure, or both at once. The name is shared by all of them. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: more than one answer. The name comes before the map. Back tomorrow, same hill.
